result: The authors developed HIV-AFMACS, an HIV reporter virus displaying a streptavidin-binding affinity tag (SBP-ΔLNGFR) at the surface of infected cells. The optimal construct (pNL4-3-ΔEnv-Nef-P2A-SBP-ΔLNGFR) expresses the tag early in infection and enables one-step magnetic bead selection with ≥90% purity from mixed populations containing 20-40% infected cells, with ≤10% loss in flow-through.
evaluation: Claims C1-C44, C151-C153 collectively demonstrate successful development and validation of HIV-AFMACS. Multiple construct designs were tested (C27-C36), with the P2A-linked version showing optimal early expression (C38-C40). High purity enrichment (≥90%) was consistently achieved in both cell lines and primary T cells (C42-C43, C151), validated by flow cytometry (C152-C153). The construct design is well-documented with sequence availability (C44).

result: The authors generated a high-coverage temporal proteomic atlas of HIV-infected primary human CD4+ T cells, quantitating approximately 9,070 proteins across 10 conditions. The time course experiment captured T cell activation effects (29% of proteins changing >2-fold) and HIV-dependent changes, with temporal profiles distinguishing Vpr substrates (depleted by 24hr in infected and partially in uninfected cells) from Vif/Nef/Vpu substrates (progressively depleted 24-48hr only in infected cells).
evaluation: Claims C3-C4, C19, C23, C45-C57, C93-C97, C118 provide comprehensive evidence for the temporal proteomic atlas. The study quantitated ~9,000 proteins (C4, C45) with appropriate controls for T cell activation (C46). Known accessory protein substrates showed expected depletion patterns (C47-C53), and temporal profiling successfully distinguished Vpr effects (early, in all cells) from other accessory proteins (late, infected cells only) (C93-C97). This represents the first high-coverage atlas in primary T cells (C118).

result: In a single time point experiment across three donors with WT and ΔVif viruses, the authors quantitated 8,789 proteins and identified 650 significantly regulated by HIV infection (q<0.05). Known accessory protein-dependent changes accounted for 297/650 (46%) of regulated proteins, including 175/299 (59%) of depleted proteins. Proteins unique to primary T cells were significantly more likely to be regulated by HIV (10.5% vs 6.9%, p<0.0001) compared to proteins detected in both primary T cells and CEM-T4s.
evaluation: Claims C5, C59-C68, C74-C75, C83-C84, C120 demonstrate robust multi-donor validation with appropriate statistical analysis. The study quantitated 8,789 proteins with 650 significantly regulated (C65-C66), showing high correlation with CEM-T4 data despite greater variability (C67-C68). Known accessory protein targets accounted for nearly half of changes (C74-C75), and statistical testing confirmed primary T cell-specific proteins are more likely to be HIV-regulated (C120). The inclusion of ΔVif virus enabled Vif-dependent analysis (C62-C64).

result: The authors identified ARID5A and PTPN22 as novel HIV targets specific to primary T cells, not detected or regulated in CEM-T4s. Both proteins were consistently depleted across all donors with fold change >2 (9-14 unique peptides), validated by immunoblot. Based on temporal regulation patterns, ARID5A and PTPN22 are very likely novel Vpr substrates, consistent with ARID5B (another ARID family member) being a conserved Vpr target.
evaluation: Claims C6-C8, C90-C92, C98-C99 provide strong evidence for ARID5A and PTPN22 as novel primary T cell-specific targets. The proteins were identified with high peptide coverage (C90), showed consistent depletion across donors (C91), and were validated by orthogonal immunoblot (C92). Temporal profiling strongly suggests Vpr-mediated targeting (C98), supported by analogy to ARID5B (C99). The inference of Vpr-dependence is reasonable but requires direct validation with ΔVpr virus.

result: The authors identified DPH7 and FMR1 as novel Vif substrates in both primary T cells and CEM-T4s. Both proteins showed Vif-dependent depletion in WT vs ΔVif infections (validated by immunoblot) and in cells transduced with Vif alone, demonstrating Vif is both necessary and sufficient for their depletion. Together with APOBEC3 and PPP2R5 family proteins/interactors, these account for all significant Vif-dependent changes in primary CD4+ T cells.
evaluation: Claims C61, C100-C114, C144 provide comprehensive evidence for DPH7 and FMR1 as Vif substrates. The proteins showed consistent Vif-dependent depletion in proteomic data (C100, C106, C108, C110), validated by immunoblot in both infection (C111) and Vif overexpression (C112) experiments. The necessity and sufficiency experiments (C113) are well-designed. The functional validation of PPP2R5 depletion via AURKB phosphorylation (C101-C105) strengthens confidence in the proteomic findings. The claim that these account for all Vif-dependent changes (C114) is well-supported.

result: Accessory proteins account for much of the proteomic remodeling in HIV-infected primary T cells. Pathways downregulated by HIV are dominated by accessory protein effects, including DNA damage response/cell cycle (Vpr), cytidine deamination/PP2A activity (Vif), and amino acid transport (Vpu/Nef). Vpr-dependent changes from CEM-T4s were recapitulated in primary T cells (32/33 substrates decreased). Upregulated proteins showed marked increases in lipid/sterol metabolism, with less concordance between cell types, likely reflecting indirect transcriptional effects.
evaluation: Claims C69-C82, C139-C142 demonstrate that accessory proteins dominate HIV-induced proteomic changes. The recapitulation of Vpr effects (C71) and pathway analysis (C76-C79) are well-supported. The observation that downregulated proteins correlate well between cell types while upregulated proteins show less concordance (C140-C142) is a reasonable interpretation. The lipid metabolism findings (C80-C82) are supported by literature and Vpr-dependence data. The overall conclusion that accessory proteins account for most changes (C139) is well-justified by the data.

result: The study validated many but not all previously reported HIV accessory protein targets. Several Nef/Vpu targets showed modest or no depletion, and no RUNX1 target gene regulation was observed. Control experiments with SBP-ΔLNGFR lentivectors showed minimal effects (37/8518 proteins, 0.4%), with only 1/650 HIV-regulated proteins (MYB) also affected by controls. Comparison with a recent study (Kuo et al. 2018) revealed that 413/650 (64%) of HIV-dependent changes identified here were obscured in that study.
evaluation: Claims C72-C73, C85-C89, C121-C126 provide important validation and comparison data. The control experiments (C86-C89) are rigorous and demonstrate that HIV-AFMACS effects are specific to HIV infection. The observation that some reported targets were not validated (C72-C73, C121-C123) is appropriately discussed with mechanistic explanations. The comparison with previous studies (C124-C126) highlights the superior depth and sensitivity of this approach. These claims strengthen confidence in the novel findings.

result: The study demonstrates methodological advantages of AFMACS over conventional approaches. Bead-based magnetic sorting is fast, simple, and scalable compared to FACS, while AFMACS avoids artifacts of antibody-based selection. The high purity (>90% infected) maximizes signal-to-noise ratio, with >90% of proteins quantitated by ≥2 unique peptides. The use of VSVg pseudotyping and Env-deficient backbone minimized artifacts (only 1/650 changes overlapped with controls) while enabling synchronous infection. Temporal profiling successfully categorized accessory protein targets despite the 24hr first timepoint limitation.
evaluation: Claims C115-C138 describe methodological strengths and limitations. The advantages of AFMACS (C115-C117) and high-purity populations (C127-C131) are well-documented. The rationale for VSVg pseudotyping (C132-C135) is sound, with appropriate controls demonstrating minimal artifacts (C134). The limitation of early timepoint analysis (C137) is acknowledged but shown to be overcome (C138). These methodological considerations strengthen confidence in the results and demonstrate careful experimental design.

result: The study is contextualized within established knowledge of viral proteome remodeling and limitations of cell line models. Primary T cells express proteins relevant to HIV infection in vivo that are absent or non-functional in cell lines (e.g., Vif, Nef, Vpu requirements; IFN restriction). The novel targets identified (ARID5A, PTPN22, DPH7, FMR1) impact processes relevant for HIV replication including inflammatory signaling, T cell activation, and translational fidelity. Further work is needed to confirm direct degradation mechanisms and identify virological phenotypes.
evaluation: Claims C9-C18, C32-C33, C58, C119, C143, C145-C150 provide appropriate context and acknowledge limitations. The rationale for using primary T cells (C15-C18, C119) is well-justified by literature. The discussion of novel target functions (C146-C149) is supported by citations. The acknowledgment that further work is needed (C145) is appropriate and honest. These claims demonstrate proper contextualization of the work within the field and realistic assessment of what has been accomplished versus what remains to be done.
